topic.name: The School Boy
topic.description: Blake's poem contrasts a boy's love of rising on a summer morning, with birds and a huntsman's horn for company, against the dread of going to school -- and ends as an appeal to his parents not to let sorrow and cares strip the joy from a young plant before it can bear fruit.

concepts.name: William Blake, the poet
concepts.description: The poem is signed with its poet's name directly beneath the final stanza.
concepts.definition: The poem 'The School Boy' is written by William Blake.

concepts.name: Rising in a summer morn
concepts.description: The boy describes how he loves to rise in summer, with birds singing on every tree, a distant huntsman's horn, and the skylark singing along with him.
concepts.definition: I love to rise in a summer morn, when the birds sing on every tree, the distant huntsman winds his horn, and the skylark sings with me.

concepts.name: School drives all joy away
concepts.description: Going to school on a summer morning is what drives all his joy away, under what the poem calls a cruel eye outworn.
concepts.definition: But to go to school on a summer morn, O it drives all joy away.

concepts.name: Sighing and dismay
concepts.description: Under the cruel eye of school, the little ones spend their day in sighing and dismay.
concepts.definition: The little ones spend the day in sighing and dismay.

concepts.name: Nor in my book can I take delight
concepts.description: Drooping in his seat, he cannot take delight in his book nor sit at ease in learning, worn through by the dreary hours.
concepts.definition: Nor in my book can I take delight, nor sit in learning's bower.

concepts.name: A bird born for joy, caged
concepts.description: The boy asks how a bird born for joy can sing sitting in a cage, and how a child, once fear troubles him, can do anything but droop and forget his youthful spring -- the comparison the whole poem turns on.
concepts.definition: Can the bird that is born for joy sit in a cage and sing? How can a child, when fears annoy, but droop his tender wing.

concepts.name: Father and Mother, if buds are nip'd
concepts.description: The final stanza is addressed directly to his father and mother, warning that if buds are nipped and blossoms blown away before their time, the summer cannot arise in joy or bear fruit.
concepts.definition: O Father and Mother, if buds are nipped, and blossoms blown away, and if the tender plants are stripped of their joy, how shall the summer arise in joy, or the summer fruits appear?
